items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

A study published in Science says the Barnes Ice Cap on Canada’s Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began expanding about 2,000 years ago. Researchers identify that growth as the start of a new glacial period. The ice began retreating around 1960 as summer warming caused it to lose more ice than it gained. The team reconstructed the ice cap’s history using vegetation preserved beneath the ice and dates from exposed rocks. The researchers define the start of a glacial period as the resumption of ice-sheet growth, differing from models that place the next glaciation thousands or tens of thousands of years in the future. Models cited by the researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. The researchers say rising atmospheric carbon dioxide makes a return to glacial conditions extremely unlikely.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Supreme Court agrees to review Trudeau government’s Emergencies Act use
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada agreed on Oct. 22 to hear the federal government’s appeal over its 2022 use of the Emergencies Act during protests in Ottawa and at key border crossings. Two lower courts found the invocation unjustified and ruled that it infringed Charter rights. The Supreme Court will also hear cross-appeals on issues raised by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Canadian Constitution Foundation. The government argues that the lower courts judged its decision with hindsight instead of asking whether officials acted reasonably on the information available at the time. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association says Ottawa is trying to relitigate arguments the courts already rejected. A public inquiry reached a different conclusion from the courts, finding in early 2023 that the government met the high legal threshold, though its commissioner said the factual basis was not overwhelming. No hearing date has been set; a hearing is unlikely before spring 2027 and could take place in the fall.

items.title: [Fast Company] The U.S. Treasury wants expanded restrictions on high-tech investments to these ‘countries of concern’
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The U.S. Treasury Department proposed a rule Thursday to crack down on American high-tech investments such as supercomputing and artificial intelligence in China, Russia, North Korea and other “countries of concern.”

The U.S. government has been working for years to deny China and other adversaries investments that could help them boost their military power.

That program began in 2023 when then-President Joe Biden signed an executive order putting restrictions on outbound U.S. investments in sectors such as semiconductors, quantum computing and artificial intelligence going into China. Treasury later established the Outbound Investment Security Program.

In December 2025, Congress passed a law that codified and expanded the program to target more technologies and more foreign countries, including Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia.

The inclusion of Russia in the proposed rule has come days after President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russia following a diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin.

The rule announced Thursday would expand the restrictions to cover investments in hypersonic systems capable of traveling at five times the speed of sound, supercomputing, biotechnology and artificial intelligence, though Treasury used Trump’s favored term for AI, “superintelligence” or SI.

The proposed rule “sends an important signal to markets that Washington is tracking where U.S. capital is flowing and what capabilities it is helping build,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

The screening of outbound investments “recognizes that capital can accelerate military-relevant capabilities just as surely as technology transfer can,” Singleton said.

Jason Chipman, a former Justice Department lawyer who specializes in cybersecurity, investment rules and export controls as a partner at the law firm WilmerHale, said the new rule “will require more substantial compliance programs to manage risk.”

Treasury’s rule to implement the 2025 law — the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act — would only apply to investments that exceed $50,000 and would exclude many financial investments, including stock purchases.

Treasury will hear public comments on the proposal before issuing a final rule.

“It’s just the first step in a fairly long process to get to changes which presumably will be more enforcement-minded, to put more teeth behind the outbound investment program,” said former U.S. trade official Ryan Majerus, now a partner at King & Spalding law firm.

In Beijing, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said the U.S. should abide by the principles of a market economy and stop interfering in normal economic and trade cooperation between businesses.

Asked about Washington’s proposal to add biotechnology to the list, ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said that “Overstretching the concept of national security, taking discriminatory measures against specific countries, and artificially restricting trade, economic and investment activities serve no one’s interests.”

She added that China will closely monitor relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

Since Trump’s first term, the United States and China — the world’s two biggest economies — have been locked in an economic and tech rivalry. They’ve restricted the export of sensitive technology and critical products — such as China’s rare earth minerals and America’s advanced computer chips — to each other and slapped tariffs on each other’s products. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed last year to ease tensions while they engaged in talks, a temporary truce they last month extended into January.

But the sparring continues. In July, the Treasury Department issued a $200,000 fine against a U.S.-based company for failing to report to the department a $92,500 investment in a Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics company by one of its subsidiaries.

—Paul Wiseman and Didi Tang, Associated Press

items.title: [livescience.com] Polar ice melt is making Earth’s solid surface rounder
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Melting polar ice is making Earth’s solid surface rounder at an accelerating rate, according to research published in the journal JGR Solid Earth. Satellite-navigation measurements show that between 2011 and 2015, the poles rose and the equatorial bulge shrank by about 0.5 to 1 millimeter per year as ice loss eased pressure on the polar crust and meltwater added mass near the equator. The study examined the solid Earth. When ocean water is included, Earth as a whole is becoming flatter by about 0.8 millimeter a year because water accumulates toward the equator.

items.title: [Fast Company] Consuming political news can hurt your job performance
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

With the midterm elections around the corner, political anxiety is in season—and productivity could pay the price.

A new study from researchers at Texas A&M University shows that consuming political news and social media outside of work affects employees’ emotional states and workplace behavior, even if they aren’t discussing politics at the water cooler.

Researchers tracked more than 300 workers over nine weeks during the 2024 presidential primary season, asking them to report how often they consumed political information, whether they viewed it as positive or negative, and how engaged, anxious, hopeful, and helpful they felt at work.

During weeks when workers consumed political information that they perceived as negative, they tended to report higher anxiety and lower engagement. During weeks when they consumed more political news that they saw as positive, they reported stronger engagement and greater willingness to help coworkers.

The takeaway is that the broader political environment affects the workplace even when politics aren’t directly discussed at the office. 

“Political information is designed to capture attention and provoke emotional reactions,” the study’s lead author, Ian Hughes, an assistant professor of psychological and brain sciences, said in a statement. “Those reactions don’t necessarily disappear once people close an app or turn off the TV.”

Organizations should be aware that employees are often dealing with additional stress during election season, he added.

“Political information has emotional consequences,” he said. “Those emotions can affect other parts of life, and that includes work.”

The study recommends that organizations provide mental health resources and support for stress management. Managers can reduce political stress by providing time off for voting or encouraging volunteering, which can increase employees’ sense of agency and control.

Workers should also engage in leisure and recovery activities, pursue “resource-building” practices such as mindfulness, gratitude, and sleep, and take breaks from media consumption.

The bank had already eliminated about 1,000 roles in the first half of the year, and about 60% of the cuts are expected to affect support functions, including development (euronews.com, bbc.co.uk, ft.com). It incurred £307 million in restructuring costs during the first nine months of 2026 (ft.com, cnbc.com). Chief Executive C. S. Venkatakrishnan said the changes build on years of technology investment, with AI expected to play a larger role as the bank modernises its infrastructure.
